title: System Reboot Frequency Anomaly
exclusions: Detects an unusually large number of distinct Linux kernel boot identities for one stable Splunk `host` during the preceding rolling 24 hours, relative to that host's coverage-qualified prior 28 complete UTC days and an absolute floor. It does not count generic `reboot`, `shutdown`, `panic`, or startup strings; infer who or what initiated a restart; prove a clean shutdown, crash, power loss, intrusion, service impact, or successful recovery; detect a service, container, pod, process, firmware, BMC, or application restart as a host reboot; or treat suspend/resume as a boot. It cannot observe a boot during which the forwarder never starts, and a restored running-machine snapshot can repeat an old boot ID. wtmp and persistent-journal records are corroboration with separate retention and writer semantics, not interchangeable identities or proof of completeness. Missing collection, an immature baseline, clock defects, duplicate host identity, and malformed fields fail closed. This operational detector is not regulatory attestation and performs no reboot, isolation, or remediation.
evidence: After deployment, retain the versioned `linux_system_reboot_frequency_anomaly` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch and triggered-result history; the exact `linux_boot_id_input` collector and checksum; effective `inputs.conf` and `props.conf`; expected-host and source-health reports; and baseline-policy approval. For each finding preserve `host`, recent distinct boot IDs, first and last boot epochs, last observed boot ID/epoch, rolling-24-hour reboot count, 28-day eligible-day count, daily mean, standard deviation, p95, calculated threshold, recent and latest-day sample counts, and search time. Link the row to raw boot snapshots, `last reboot`/wtmp retained-range output, `journalctl --list-boots` and selected `_BOOT_ID` records where available, kernel/crash/pstore, hypervisor/cloud/BMC, change, cluster-drain, incident, and dated positive/negative control evidence. These artifacts show what the documented feed and SPL evaluated; this documentation-only review created no runtime evidence and does not establish reboot cause, source completeness, production suitability, or compliance.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Freeze `now()` at 12:00 UTC in an isolated index and create 24 complete historical baseline days for `host=reboot-frequency-positive`, each with at least 230 unique five-minute `sourcetype=linux:boot_id source=linux_boot_id` observations, valid UUIDs, and one old boot whose `boot_time_epoch` precedes the 28-day baseline; therefore every eligible historical day has `daily_reboots=0`. During the final rolling 24 hours emit at least 230 observations spanning three successive valid boot IDs whose kernel boot epochs all fall inside that window. Run the catalogue SPL with only the index changed. Expect exactly one high-severity row with `reboots_last_24h=3`, `baseline_days=24`, mean/stdev/p95 of 0, and `alert_threshold=3`; repeated observations of each UUID must count once.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Under the same fixed clock and source contract, run independent fixtures and expect zero rows for: two distinct boot IDs in the final 24 hours against a zero baseline; thousands of repeated events carrying one boot ID; syslog text containing `reboot`, `shutdown`, `kernel panic`, or `Restarting system` but no boot-identity events; three recent IDs with fewer than 230 unique observation epochs; fewer than 14 coverage-qualified historical days; a malformed UUID; a boot epoch after its observation time by more than 600 seconds; and three recent boots when a valid high-variance baseline produces a calculated threshold above three. Confirm source-health and baseline-readiness searches expose low coverage and immature history rather than reporting a healthy zero.

dataSources: Primary analytical feed: the deployment-owned `linux_boot_id_input` Universal Forwarder scripted input used by UC-1.1.20, writing one key-value observation every 300 seconds to the local convention `index=os`, `source=linux_boot_id`, and `sourcetype=linux:boot_id`. Splunk supplies `_time` and `host`; the collector reads `boot_id` from `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` and `boot_time_epoch` (`btime`) from `/proc/stat`. The kernel documents boot ID as a UUID that remains unchanged for one boot, so the search counts distinct identities rather than log lines. Required source-side corroboration for qualification and triage is util-linux `last reboot` over `/var/log/wtmp` plus systemd journal `_BOOT_ID`/`journalctl --list-boots` where persistent journal exists. wtmp can be absent, rotated, truncated, disabled, or incomplete and has no kernel boot UUID; journal retention can also omit boots. Neither source is silently unioned into the distinct-ID count.
app: A locally managed `linux_boot_id_input` app containing the read-only POSIX collector, five-minute Universal Forwarder scripted-input stanza, and key-value source-type configuration, plus a search app containing this saved search and dashboards. No premium app or Splunkbase add-on is required. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) is optional for `Unix:Uptime` and adjacent host context; it does not supply the `linux:boot_id` contract or make generic syslog reboot phrases safe to count.
spl:
index=os source=linux_boot_id sourcetype="linux:boot_id" earliest=-36d@d latest=-5m@m
| fields _time host boot_id boot_time_epoch
| eval boot_id=lower(trim(boot_id)), boot_time_epoch=tonumber(boot_time_epoch)
| where isnotnull(host) AND match(boot_id,"^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$") AND boot_time_epoch>0 AND boot_time_epoch<=_time+600
| dedup host boot_id boot_time_epoch _time
| eventstats dc(eval(if(_time>=now()-86400 AND _time<now(),_time,null()))) as recent_samples dc(eval(if(boot_time_epoch>=now()-86400 AND boot_time_epoch<now(),boot_id,null()))) as reboots_last_24h values(eval(if(boot_time_epoch>=now()-86400 AND boot_time_epoch<now(),boot_id,null()))) as recent_boot_ids min(eval(if(boot_time_epoch>=now()-86400 AND boot_time_epoch<now(),boot_time_epoch,null()))) as first_recent_boot_epoch max(eval(if(boot_time_epoch>=now()-86400 AND boot_time_epoch<now(),boot_time_epoch,null()))) as last_recent_boot_epoch by host
| eval observation_day=floor(_time/86400)*86400, boot_day=floor(boot_time_epoch/86400)*86400, today_utc=floor(now()/86400)*86400, daily_marker=mvappend("coverage|" . observation_day . "|" . _time,"boot|" . boot_day . "|" . boot_id)
| mvexpand daily_marker
| rex field=daily_marker "^(?<marker_type>coverage|boot)\|(?<utc_day>[0-9]+)\|(?<marker_value>.+)$"
| eval utc_day=tonumber(utc_day), daily_sample_epoch=if(marker_type="coverage",tonumber(marker_value),null()), daily_boot_id=if(marker_type="boot",marker_value,null())
| stats dc(daily_sample_epoch) as daily_samples dc(daily_boot_id) as daily_reboots latest(boot_id) as latest_boot_id latest(boot_time_epoch) as latest_boot_epoch latest(recent_samples) as recent_samples latest(reboots_last_24h) as reboots_last_24h latest(recent_boot_ids) as recent_boot_ids latest(first_recent_boot_epoch) as first_recent_boot_epoch latest(last_recent_boot_epoch) as last_recent_boot_epoch latest(today_utc) as today_utc by host utc_day
| eval baseline_eligible=if(utc_day>=today_utc-(28*86400) AND utc_day<today_utc AND daily_samples>=230,1,0)
| eventstats count(eval(if(baseline_eligible=1,daily_reboots,null()))) as baseline_days avg(eval(if(baseline_eligible=1,daily_reboots,null()))) as baseline_mean stdev(eval(if(baseline_eligible=1,daily_reboots,null()))) as baseline_stdev perc95(eval(if(baseline_eligible=1,daily_reboots,null()))) as baseline_p95 by host
| where utc_day=today_utc
| eval baseline_stdev=coalesce(baseline_stdev,0), statistical_limit=ceil(max(baseline_mean+(3*baseline_stdev),baseline_p95+1)), alert_threshold=max(3,statistical_limit)
| where baseline_days>=14 AND recent_samples>=230 AND reboots_last_24h>=alert_threshold
| eval baseline_mean=round(baseline_mean,2), baseline_stdev=round(baseline_stdev,2), baseline_p95=round(baseline_p95,2), first_recent_boot_time=strftime(first_recent_boot_epoch,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"), last_recent_boot_time=strftime(last_recent_boot_epoch,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"), latest_boot_time=strftime(latest_boot_epoch,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z"), severity="high", use_case="UC-1.1.118"
| table host severity reboots_last_24h alert_threshold baseline_days baseline_mean baseline_stdev baseline_p95 recent_samples daily_samples recent_boot_ids first_recent_boot_epoch first_recent_boot_time last_recent_boot_epoch last_recent_boot_time latest_boot_id latest_boot_epoch latest_boot_time use_case
| sort 0 -reboots_last_24h host
description: Reports a Linux host when at least three distinct kernel boot UUIDs occurred during the preceding rolling 24 hours and that count also meets or exceeds the larger of the host's prior 28-day daily mean plus three standard deviations or prior p95 plus one. Only coverage-qualified historical days form the baseline, at least 14 such days and 230 recent five-minute observations are required, and repeated messages or repeated samples of one boot count once.
value: Repeated host boots can signal a crash loop, failed patch, unstable hardware, power interruption, broken orchestration, or recovery action that is eroding availability. Boot-identity counting prevents noisy startup text from multiplying one restart, while a per-host baseline avoids applying the same normal frequency to immutable workers and long-lived databases. Coverage and minimum-count guards give platform teams an actionable investigation queue without presenting missing telemetry or a young baseline as statistical confidence.
implementation: Reuse or deploy the UC-1.1.20 `linux_boot_id_input` collector at a five-minute interval, verify the UUID and kernel `btime` contract against each supported Linux host class, and operate separate expected-host freshness monitoring. Preserve wtmp and persistent journal where local policy permits and qualify their retention as corroboration, not as replacements for boot identity. Save this SPL as `linux_system_reboot_frequency_anomaly`, schedule it every 15 minutes with a five-minute close delay, and trigger on returned rows. The initial policy requires at least three distinct boots in 24 hours, 14 of 28 prior days with at least 230 samples, and a threshold above both mean-plus-three-standard-deviations and p95-plus-one; review those catalogue defaults against host role and incident history before production paging.
visualization: Use a latest-findings table with host, rolling-24-hour distinct boots, calculated threshold, baseline days, mean, standard deviation, p95, coverage counts, recent boot IDs, and first/last/current boot times. Add a 35-day per-host UTC-day reboot-count chart with the dynamic threshold, a boot-interval timeline, and aligned change/incident annotations. Place source health above the findings: expected hosts, latest sample age, daily sample completeness, UUID/epoch validation failures, shared-host identity, and baseline readiness. Add drilldowns to raw boot snapshots, `last reboot`, journal boot list and selected prior boot, kernel/pstore/crash data, hypervisor/cloud/BMC lifecycle, cluster drains, and changes. Never chart raw message count as reboot count or label missing collection as zero reboots.
schema: Custom Linux kernel boot-identity observations; wtmp and systemd journal boot records are source-side corroboration
dataModelAcceleration: No documented Splunk Common Information Model dataset preserves Linux kernel boot UUID, kernel boot epoch, five-minute observation coverage, and the zero-reboot host-day series required by this baseline. Generic Availability or Change events and `Unix:Uptime` do not provide the same identity contract. There is no faithful `tstats` substitute. At fleet scale, a reviewed summary index may retain one row per host/UTC day with distinct boot count, sample count, first/last boot epoch, and source-health state, but it must preserve zero days, late-event handling, host identity, and links to raw observations before replacing this SPL.

knownFalsePositives:
A qualifying row represents multiple distinct boot identities under the documented host and coverage contract. "False positive" therefore means the boots are expected, the host identity or boot epoch is wrong, or the statistical policy is unsuitable—not that backup I/O, a monitoring poll, or a repeated syslog line resembles a reboot.

1. **Approved patch, kernel, firmware, or security reboot campaign** — Configuration management may intentionally cycle a host several times while testing packages, rollback, initramfs, or firmware. Correlate every recent boot epoch with the exact host, change, automation run, owner, expected count, and bounded UTC window. Retain the anomaly as change evidence; suppress only notification delivery for that host/window.

2. **High-availability, cluster, or immutable-node lifecycle** — Node drains, image replacement, autoscaling, spot/preemptible capacity, disaster-recovery exercises, and lab rebuilds can make frequent boots normal for a role. Confirm stable asset/instance identity and service availability. Prefer a separately approved host-class policy or exclusion from this long-lived-host detector; do not raise every server's threshold to accommodate ephemeral workers.

3. **Crash-loop, boot-loop, resilience, watchdog, or power-fail test** — An authorized exercise deliberately creates real repeated boots. Require an isolated target, safety approval, test plan, expected boot count, stop condition, owner, and time-bounded ticket. Preserve unsuppressed raw and control results. Unexpected continuation after the test is actionable.

4. **Two machines sharing one Splunk `host`** — Cloned images, reused `serverName`, conflicting host transforms, or overlapping forwarding routes can interleave different boot UUIDs and fabricate high frequency. Compare forwarder GUID, cloud instance or VM identity, restricted machine inventory, source route, boot epochs, and simultaneous samples. Repair identity immediately; never add a permanent exception for a collision.

5. **VM snapshot restore, checkpoint/restore, or hostname reuse** — Restoring a running VM can reintroduce a previously observed boot UUID and old boot epoch; replacing an instance under the same host label can introduce a new UUID without being an in-place reboot. Compare hypervisor/cloud task history, instance generation, boot epoch, wtmp retained range, journal list, and collector continuity. A repeated old UUID can make distinct-count frequency undercount rather than overcount, so route snapshot restores to continuity review.

6. **Clock or timestamp defect** — A bad real-time clock, time step, cloned guest state, or incorrect `_time` assignment can move `btime` into the wrong UTC day or outside the rolling window. The SPL rejects boot epochs more than 600 seconds after observation but cannot prove all old epochs are correct. Compare `/proc/stat`, current UTC, uptime, journal monotonic/realtime context, NTP state, and hypervisor clock before accepting the count.

7. **Threshold mismatch after role change** — A rebuilt test host may legitimately have a different reboot distribution than its preceding database role while retaining the same host key. Baseline history then mixes unlike populations. Reset or version the analytical identity through governed inventory, allow at least 14 qualified days to mature, and document the new role; do not let old variance silently authorize a reboot storm.

**Safe suppression:** keep the catalogue SPL and base result intact. If local policy permits temporary notification suppression, apply a post-result lookup such as `linux_reboot_frequency_exceptions.csv` keyed by exact `host` and `use_case`, with numeric `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, expected purpose, and maximum expected boot count. Reject wildcards, open-ended/expired rows, and exceptions for source-health, host-collision, malformed-epoch, or immature-baseline conditions. Re-page when the observed count exceeds the approved test count or the exception expires.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational Linux availability and reliability anomaly; reboot frequency alone does not establish adversary behavior)
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Linux kernel boot_id/proc-stat, util-linux last/wtmp, systemd journal boot identity, and Splunk statistical/search/input sources; synthetic controls and runtime reconciliation specified but not executed; no live Splunk, fleet, crash-loop, hypervisor, wtmp-retention, production, or SME validation

cost.search_load_notes: A five-minute heartbeat produces about 288 small events per host per day. The direct search scans 36 days, deduplicates observations, builds covered UTC-day counts, and calculates per-host statistics; large fleets should validate concurrency and summarize only after preserving zero-day and coverage semantics.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and semantic boundary

Assign Linux platform, Splunk collection/search, availability, change, virtualization/cloud, and service owners. Implement and validate UC-1.1.20 first because this use case consumes the same kernel boot-identity observations and adds history, coverage, and statistics. The forwarder account needs only execute access to the reviewed collector and read access to `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` and `/proc/stat`; test under the actual systemd sandbox, container/procfs namespace, SELinux/AppArmor policy, and distribution. It needs no root shell, `sudo`, wtmp write access, journal-vacuum permission, reboot privilege, or network listener. The search role needs read access to `index=os` and permission to schedule the saved search.

Treat identity, time, frequency, and cause as separate facts. Linux documents `boot_id` as a UUID that remains unchanged for one running kernel. `/proc/stat` `btime` assigns that boot to an epoch. Repeated five-minute observations of one UUID remain one boot. Generic text such as `reboot`, `shutdown`, `Restarting system`, `kernel panic`, or a service startup can be absent, repeated, localized, replayed, or unrelated and is never the count denominator. A new UUID does not prove clean shutdown, panic, power loss, intrusion, or impact. Suspend/resume normally retains the UUID. Common containers share the host kernel identity. One stable Splunk `host` must represent one machine lifecycle; two machines sharing a host key fabricate frequency.

wtmp and the systemd journal are corroboration, not alternate count keys. `last reboot` reads special reboot records from wtmp, but wtmp writers and retention determine what exists; removal, rotation, truncation, image replacement, or a boot that never reaches the writer can omit history. wtmp has no kernel boot UUID. Journal `_BOOT_ID` carries the kernel identity, and `journalctl --list-boots` lists only retained boots. A volatile or vacuumed journal is incomplete. Never add collector, wtmp, and journal counts together because one boot can appear in all three.

## Step 1 — Deploy and qualify collection

Package `scriptExample` as `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_boot_id_input/bin/boot_id.sh`, writable only by deployment administration and executable by the forwarder identity. It emits one key-value line and exits nonzero on an unreadable or malformed source. Do not convert failure to an empty UUID or epoch zero; no event is unknown coverage, not no reboot.

Configure `local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_boot_id_input/bin/boot_id.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 300
index = os
source = linux_boot_id
sourcetype = linux:boot_id
```

A numeric Splunk interval starts after the prior invocation completes, so 300 seconds is a target cadence. One continuously observed host produces about 288 small events per day. The rule accepts 230 unique observation epochs as roughly 80% coverage. Measure runtime, indexing delay, duplicates, and actual ingest. A short boot during which the forwarder never launches cannot be represented by this feed; reconciliation must expose that gap.

Configure the applicable parsing/search tiers:

```ini
[linux:boot_id]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)
TRUNCATE = 1024
DATETIME_CONFIG = CURRENT
KV_MODE = auto
```

Keep `_time` as observation time. Do not rewrite it to `boot_time_epoch`, because that would collapse the heartbeat and remove evidence for zero-reboot days. Inspect winning settings with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and `splunk btool props list linux:boot_id --debug`. Run the collector as the service account; compare with the native Linux interface at `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` and the `btime` line in `/proc/stat`. Search 15 minutes and confirm approximately three uniquely timed events with stable UUID/epoch, exact metadata, correct host identity, and acceptable `_indextime-_time` delay.

On each supported host class, run `last --time-format iso reboot`, record `wtmp begins`, and verify which wtmp file and writers are in use. On systemd hosts run `journalctl --list-boots`; compare current `_BOOT_ID` with the collector after accounting for hyphen presentation, and document whether journal storage is persistent plus its vacuum limits. There is no Linux vendor UI for this contract; these native host interfaces, then hypervisor/cloud/BMC consoles, are the source-side comparison points. Current-boot disagreement blocks deployment until identity, clock, namespace, restore, and parsing are resolved.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the SPL

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_system_reboot_frequency_anomaly`, run it every 15 minutes, trigger when results are greater than zero, and retain the five-minute close delay. The 36-day range supplies 28 complete UTC baseline days plus margin. Capacity-test host count and dispatch concurrency. Do not shorten history while continuing to claim 28 days, and do not summarize only reboot days.

The opening commands enforce the source contract, normalize UUID case, cast `btime`, reject malformed identities and a boot epoch more than 600 seconds after observation, and deduplicate exact observations. `eventstats` counts distinct IDs whose kernel epoch is in the previous 86,400 seconds and separately counts recent observation epochs. Repeated samples do not inflate frequency.

Every source event creates two multivalue markers: a coverage marker assigned to the UTC day of `_time`, and a boot marker assigned to the UTC day of `boot_time_epoch`. `mvexpand` and `rex` produce aligned rows. `stats` then counts observation epochs and boot IDs independently. This preserves a reboot just before midnight whose first forwarded event arrives after midnight. Continuous collection also creates a daily row with `daily_reboots=0`, preventing the upward bias caused by averaging only days containing boot events.

A prior day is eligible only when it is one of the previous 28 complete UTC days and has at least 230 unique samples. The search calculates the count of eligible days, mean, sample standard deviation, and p95 from those daily values. At least 14 eligible days and 230 samples in the current rolling 24 hours are required. Missing or immature data fails closed and belongs in health reporting.

The threshold is the greatest of 3, `ceil(mean + 3 × stdev)`, and `ceil(p95 + 1)`; equality breaches. Three is an absolute operational floor, p95-plus-one requires movement beyond the historical high percentile, and mean-plus-three-standard-deviations accounts for spread. This transparent heuristic is not a Linux or Splunk default, does not prove Gaussian data, and must be reviewed by host role. Daily counts are discrete and often zero-inflated. Replace it only with separately tested seasonal or robust logic, and never pool unlike hosts into one baseline.

Route the high-severity result by exact `host,use_case`, retain every dispatch, and suppress duplicate notification for no more than one schedule. The alert must not reboot, drain, isolate, roll back, change a watchdog, or modify cluster state.

## Step 3 — Validate identity, zeros, thresholds, and coverage

Execute the exact positive and negative `controlTest` fixtures with fixed `now()` and absolute epochs. Historical zero days still need at least 230 source events. Inspect each pipeline gate: contract validation, deduplication, rolling distinct IDs, recent coverage, marker expansion, UTC-day counts, eligible days, statistics, threshold, and result. The positive zero baseline must yield mean 0, stdev 0, p95 0, threshold 3, and exactly one result for three recent IDs.

Test two versus three recent IDs; current count one below and exactly equal to a higher dynamic threshold; baselines with occasional one-, two-, and high-count days; 229 versus 230 samples; 13 versus 14 eligible days; uppercase and malformed UUIDs; +600 versus +601-second future boot epoch; exact duplicates; delayed indexing; a boot exactly 24 hours old; and a boot immediately before UTC midnight first observed after midnight. Confirm the current partial day never enters the prior baseline.

On an authorized nonproduction host, capture UUID and btime, perform one planned reboot, and compare the next sample with `/proc`, `last reboot`, `journalctl --list-boots`, selected current/previous `_BOOT_ID` records, and the hypervisor or cloud operation. Additional reboots to reach the threshold require a lab safety/change plan. Synthetic events validate SPL, not kernel, wtmp, journal, startup, crash capture, or host identity. Do not crash-loop production to test an alert.

Operate a separate expected-host health search for latest observation age, sample completeness, invalid UUID/epoch, ID changing without btime, btime changing without ID, simultaneous IDs under one host, indexing delay, missing expected hosts, and baseline readiness. Reconcile collector IDs with journal IDs and compare epochs with wtmp. A quiet anomaly search without healthy source and baseline reports is unknown, not stable.

Keep `status=draft` until a qualified operator executes controls, source reconciliation, search-performance tests, and host-role threshold review. This editorial review did not run SPL, ingest fixtures, reboot a host, or inspect production retention.

## Step 4 — Operationalize triage and evidence

Build the views in `visualization`, placing source health and baseline readiness above findings. Plot daily zeros, preserve recent IDs, and annotate patches, cluster drains, image replacement, watchdog tests, power events, and incidents. Ephemeral workers need stable instance identity and a separate lifecycle policy rather than a long-lived hostname baseline.

For a finding, first prove one machine owns the host key. Compare every recent UUID and btime with raw snapshots, wtmp retained range, journal boot list, and hypervisor/cloud/BMC lifecycle. Then distinguish planned maintenance from watchdog, panic/oops/crash dump, pstore, hardware/RAS, power/UPS, storage/root-filesystem, OOM/resource exhaustion, and orchestration behavior. A missing shutdown record can support an unclean-stop hypothesis but cannot prove it because writer and retention failure produce the same absence.

Assess service impact independently through quorum, drain/failover state, boot duration, failed units, filesystem recovery, application readiness, traffic, errors, latency, and lost jobs. Reboot frequency alone is not adversary attribution. Escalate security only with independent evidence.

Apply only exact, expiring, post-result notification exceptions described in `knownFalsePositives`. Preserve raw events, base results, statistics, source health, and the decision. Planned tests must state a maximum expected boot count and re-page when exceeded. Never suppress host collision, malformed timestamps, collector silence, or an immature baseline.

Retain the artifacts named in `evidence` under local operations, security, and privacy policy. Version collector, source type, search, summary logic, expected-host inventory, threshold decision, and exceptions. Revalidate after kernel, init/systemd, wtmp/journal, image, virtualization, forwarder, parsing, naming, schedule, or statistical changes.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot source-specific failures

- **No events:** run the collector as the forwarder user; verify procfs visibility, execute permission, app deployment, input, route, index, role, and `ExecProcessor` messages. Do not fall back to counting syslog words.
- **Null fields:** inspect `_raw`, exact source type, and winning `KV_MODE=auto`; this is one key-value line, not a multikv table.
- **UUID changes every sample:** verify the script reads `boot_id`, not `/proc/sys/kernel/random/uuid`, and check for two machines sharing one host.
- **UUID never changes after a known reboot:** verify machine/procfs namespace, current file, forwarder startup, replay, route, host key, and VM snapshot restore.
- **Implausible boot epoch:** compare btime, current UTC, uptime, NTP, guest/hypervisor clock, snapshot history, and `_time`; preserve and reject bad values rather than applying `abs()` or now.
- **wtmp disagreement:** inspect retained beginning, rotation, removal, writers, selected file, time changes, and whether userspace reached the writer. Never join wtmp to UUID solely by nearest time.
- **Journal misses boots:** verify persistent storage, selected machine/namespace, vacuum limits, corruption, and list-boots. Volatile history cannot prove absence.
- **High count but null baseline:** inspect eligible days and coverage. New and intermittent hosts deliberately fail closed; do not lower history silently.
- **Missing zero days:** confirm coverage markers exist and `_time` remains observation time. Repair timestamping rather than filling unknown days with zero.
- **Unexpectedly large threshold:** inspect role changes, identity reuse, campaigns, and outlier days. Version analytical identity when the underlying population changes.
- **Expensive search:** inspect scanned volume, concurrency, extraction, and scheduler load. A daily summary is acceptable only after replay proves covered zeros, distinct IDs, samples, late-event revision, and raw drilldown remain intact.
- **Fleet-wide alert:** correlate patch orchestration, cloud/hypervisor control plane, power/facilities, deployment-server, certificate, and host-transform changes before opening unrelated incidents.
grandmaExplanation: We count how many genuinely new starts each Linux server has had, instead of counting repeated log messages. If a server starts at least three times in a day and that is unusually frequent for that server, the team can investigate a crash loop, failed update, power problem, or planned test.
hardware: Linux physical servers, virtual machines, and node operating systems exposing `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` and `/proc/stat`. Common containers share the host kernel boot identity and are not separate reboot entities. VM snapshot/restore and cloned host metadata require explicit lifecycle and identity qualification.
scriptExample:
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

BOOT_ID_FILE=/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
PROC_STAT=/proc/stat

boot_id=$(sed -n '1p' "$BOOT_ID_FILE")
boot_time_epoch=$(awk '$1 == "btime" {print $2; found=1; exit} END {if (!found) exit 1}' "$PROC_STAT")
case "$boot_id" in
  ????????-????-????-????-????????????) ;;
  *) exit 1 ;;
esac
case "$boot_time_epoch" in
  ''|*[!0-9]*) exit 1 ;;
esac
printf 'boot_id=%s boot_time_epoch=%s\n' "$boot_id" "$boot_time_epoch"

splunkbaseApps.name: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux
